frontmatter.title: Ripple-carry modular arithmetic
frontmatter.description: An explicit Boolean carry alternative, its space/rotation tradeoff, and an equal-task conditional resource comparison.

children.value: needs reversible modular multiplication. Fourier arithmetic stores addition in phases; ripple arithmetic carries ordinary binary information along a register using reversible Boolean gates. This variant makes the tradeoff visible: more work qubits and compiled operations, but many fewer general-angle rotations in the demonstrated circuits.

This conclusion is conditional on QDK 1.34.0’s PSSPC mean-fit angle synthesis, layout and factory models. It neither generates a concrete synthesis sequence nor certifies approximation error or runtime tails. QDK abstracts Clifford scheduling, which matters because ripple has more compiled gates and depth. The results include all supplied work qubits, preparation, controls, cleanup, final readout, serial trials and modeled factories; classical base selection, continued fractions, gcd, compilation and verification time are excluded from physical elapsed time. All qubits begin at zero in the model, with no explicit reset instructions. These numbers are not an observed physical speedup, and do not alter the frozen Grover baseline. See

The Boolean simulator interprets the actual X/CX/CCX/SWAP/CSWAP source gates using integer bit operations. It checks active and inactive controls and clean work registers without allocating an exponentially large statevector. Basis checks alone are distinguished from coherent checks: tests also compare Qiskit complex amplitudes on superpositions, including relative phase, and compare a small lowered circuit with its original statevector.
The sparse source simulator applies the actual H, phase and Boolean gates to complex amplitudes without truncation.

Input generation permits at most 12 integer bits and 24 exponent bits, with an arithmetic-work preflight and 500,000 compiled-operation cap. Source lowering is capped at 64 wires and 100,000 primitives. The quantum sparse simulator separately caps exponent precision at eight bits, support at 8,192 amplitudes and work at four million gate-state applications. Dense Qiskit checks cap both 20 wires and a separate gate-amplitude work estimate; a full N15 dense check is optional and took about 34 seconds in the recorded CPU environment. These caps reject costly requests instead of promising simulation from a circuit’s logical width.
